pass_a_gloss: I was praying therefore that you, through the whole contest standing in, remembering the much wage stored up in the heavens for those persecuted and insulted on account of justice and on account of the son of the human, would be glad and exult and skip, just as the apostles were glad once, having been deemed worthy to be dishonoured on behalf of his name. And if ever you should perceive a contraction about your soul, let the mind of Christ in us say to it, it wanting, so far as lies on itself, to pour into confusion even him: to what end are you deeply grieved, soul? and to what end do you trouble me together? put hope upon God, because I will confess to him; and again. Would that in no way the soul be troubled, but even beside the courts themselves and beside naked swords brought upon the neck it be garrisoned by the peace of God that holds above every mind, and be in a calm sea, reckoning that those going abroad out of the body go home to the very Lord of the wholes. But if we are not of such size as always to keep the untroubled state, even so let the trouble of the soul not be poured out nor shown to those outside, so that we may have space of defence-speech toward God, saying to him: my God, toward myself my soul was troubled. And the word calls on us to remember also the thing said in Isaiah in this manner: do not fear reproach of humans, and by their contempt do not be worsted. For indeed it is out of place, God standing over clearly the motion of the heaven and of the things in it and the things on land and sea completed by his divine art in comings-to-be and constitutions and feedings and growings of all-kinds of living creatures and plants, to close the eyes and not look in on God, but to turn the eyes upon fear of those after a little going to die and going to be handed over to the justice according to their worth.
pass_b_english: So I prayed that you, throughout the whole of the present contest, would remember the great reward laid up in heaven for those who are persecuted and reviled “for righteousness' sake” (Matthew 5:10) and for the sake of the Son of Man (Luke 6:22), and would rejoice and be glad and leap for joy (Luke 6:23), as the apostles once rejoiced that they had been counted worthy to be dishonoured “for his name” (Acts 5:41). And if ever you feel a shrinking in your soul, let the mind of Christ that is in us say to the soul, when it wishes, as far as lies in its power, to throw that mind into confusion as well: “Why are you so sorrowful, O soul? And why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I will give thanks to him” (Psalm 42:5); and let it say so again (Psalm 42:11).

Would that the soul were not troubled at all, but that even before the very tribunals, and with bare swords brought down upon the neck, it might be guarded by the peace of God that surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7), and be calm, reckoning that those who are away “from the body” are at home with the Lord of all himself (2 Corinthians 5:8). But if we are not so great as always to keep our calm, then at least let the soul's trouble not pour out or show itself to those outside, so that we may have room to make our defence before God, saying to him, “My God, my soul was troubled within me” (Psalm 42:6).

The Word also urges us to remember what is said in Isaiah in this way: “Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be defeated by their scorn” (Isaiah 51:7). For it is absurd, when God is plainly present over the motion of heaven and of all that is in it, and over everything his divine craft accomplishes on land and sea in the births, structures, nourishment and growth of every kind of animal and plant, to shut our eyes and not look upon God, and to turn our eyes instead to fear of those who will shortly die and be handed over to the judgment they deserve.
